children.text: Across from San Agustin Church in Intramuros, this "living museum" recreates the rooms, furniture and daily life of a wealthy Filipino family of the late 19th century. Admission is cheap and you can see it in about an hour.

Casa Manila is a museum in Plaza San Luis, Intramuros. Room by room, it shows how a Filipino family made wealthy by trade and hacienda income lived in the late Spanish colonial period. The building is in the bahay na bato style (a house of stone and wood), a traditional Philippine mansion form, and has three floors. According to its own materials, it was among the first museums in the Philippines on the theme of Spanish colonial life. It stands across from San Agustin Church, in the block bounded by General Luna, Real, Cabildo and Urdaneta streets. This area is Barrio San Luis, one of the four old villages that made up Intramuros. Admission is cheap, so it is easy to drop in, and you will enjoy it much more if you learn the names and uses of the rooms beforehand.

The façade copies the 1850s San Nicolas house, a bahay na bato mansion that stood on Jaboneros Street in Binondo. Intramuros was heavily destroyed in World War II and no Spanish-era mansions survive, so this building is a recreation built new in the 1980s from the vision of Imelda Marcos. It was designed by J. Ramon Faustmann, the project was led by Jaime Laya, then administrator of the Intramuros Administration, and it is said to have been completed around 1981 as part of the San Luis Complex. Furnishings and objects were gathered from many sources and placed by area, as they might have been in a Spanish-era house. Barrio San Luis also had other grand houses, Los Hidalgos (c. 1650) and the Cuyugan Mansion (c. 1890). It is more interesting once you know that this is not an authentic old house but a model museum built to show old life.

The furniture and decoration reflect late 19th-century tastes, with many pieces imported from Europe and China. The premise is that the household's wealth came partly from trade and partly from provincial haciendas. A traditional bahay na bato usually has two floors, with the ground level used as a carriage garage and grain warehouse; Casa Manila had too little space for that and instead has three floors. Knowing these differences makes comparing it with real houses fun.

It is small compared with the big museums, but it lets you picture a family's daily life and its culture of hospitality in concrete terms. It is a good stop in the middle of an Intramuros day, together with San Agustin Church. The Intramuros Administration has also published virtual tours (#IntramurosVirtualTours), which help if you watch them beforehand. Hours and admission arrangements sometimes differ between announcements, so be sure to check the Intramuros Administration's latest notice before you go.
The ground floor has the stone-paved passageway called the zaguan, the courtyard patio, and the caballeriza (stables), where horses were kept. It gives you a first impression of a wealthy house.

The mezzanine between the first and second floors has a waiting room for tradesmen, an office, bedrooms and the despacho, the master's business office. The despacho holds a private library and baúl mundo travel chests.

The caida (antesala) is the everyday room for receiving guests, and the sala is the main hall for large gatherings and events. The sala is said to have imported crystal chandeliers, gilded mirrors and a square grand piano.

blocks.title: The oratorio and the Blue Room

children.text: There is the oratorio, a small family chapel for prayer, and a room known as the Blue Room. They show how a household of the time kept a separate space for devotion at home.

blocks.title: The master bedroom and Kama ni Ah-Tay

children.text: The carved bed "Kama ni Ah-Tay" is said to be named after Ah-Tay, a furniture maker in Binondo. The room also explains the custom of hospitality in which the master's bedroom was given to an important guest staying the night.

The dining room ceiling has a punkah, a manual fan worked by pulling a cord, and the kitchen has a nievera, an ice box that was a 19th-century status symbol. The bathroom has stoneware bathtubs said to have come from China.
European pieces such as bentwood furniture described as coming from Vienna sit alongside a Sheraton-style side table made in Pampanga, showing foreign tastes meeting local craftsmanship.
The rooftop azotea was where household chores were done, with an aljibe (water cistern) and an herb garden. It helps you imagine a servant's day.

The dry season, November to May, is best. Casa Manila is indoors, but most of an Intramuros day is spent walking outdoors, so the less rainy months are easier.

Operating arrangements differ between announcements, so before a weekday visit check whether a reservation is needed. One official notice said Tuesday to Friday visits are for groups of 10 by reservation, booked at least two working days ahead. Weekend hours are given as 9:00–17:00.
Intramuros is best for a walk on the walls in the late afternoon, so it is efficient to schedule Casa Manila in the morning and the walls and fortress in the afternoon.

Around Casa Manila there are hotels inside Intramuros and in Ermita and Malate, which makes it easy to stay and combine with an Intramuros itinerary. Lodging inside the walls is quiet and within walking distance.

For lunch and snacks, use the restaurants and cafés inside Intramuros. Traditional Filipino food and cafés are found throughout, good for a rest after the museum. Cash may be needed for admission, so carry some small bills; check locally whether electronic payment is accepted. There is no restaurant inside the museum, so plan your meals before or after your visit.

Intramuros has so much to see that it is hard to cover in one day. A comfortable plan is to see Casa Manila in the morning, escape the heat at midday in a shaded indoor exhibit or a church, and walk the walls after the sun lowers. Parts of the walled city restrict car traffic, so it is best to leave luggage at your hotel and get around on foot.
Before you go, check the Intramuros Administration's latest hours and reservation method.
